facts.label: Readiness view
facts.text: The effective source set supports the requested work with limitations. CHS Inc. is a Minnesota agricultural cooperative whose only registered securities are five series of listed preferred stock; its borrowing is private placement notes, bank term loans and short-term facilities described in the notes to the audited statements. The annual report for fiscal 2026, three quarterly reports and three earnings releases give audited and unaudited statements, a debt table, a maturity schedule, segment tables and a statement that covenants were met. What is absent is the legal and market layer: the agreements that carry the covenants, any rating, any trading quote and any EBITDA reconciliation. The binding consequence is that financial, business and evidence-trace work can proceed on filed documents, while covenant testing and instrument-level legal analysis cannot proceed from these sources and need a further evidence action.

facts.label: Financial base view
facts.text: CHS Inc. entered fiscal 2026 with modest year-end leverage and finished with a very strong second half, when pretax income was 1,021,508 against 107,211 in the first half (C9). Derived EBITDA of 1,969,497 against total debt of 2,501,725 gives 1.27x at the 2026-08-31 balance sheet date, down from 2.12x a year earlier, and cash paid for interest of 167,057 is covered 11.79x. That picture is flattering in four ways that the base keeps in view. First, the EBITDA is our derivation (pretax income plus interest expense plus depreciation and amortization, including amortization of deferred major maintenance) because the company reports no EBITDA, and it includes 569,231 of equity income from joint ventures and affiliates. Second, nine-month operating earnings were a loss of 12,222 and the fourth quarter derived alone supplied most of the year, so the annual figure is dominated by one quarter. Third, the improvement is concentrated in one segment: Energy improved by 573,605, which exceeds the group improvement of 513,947 because Corporate and Services and Agronomy declined (C16). Fourth, working capital debt is seasonal: notes payable fell from 1,995,108 in February to 449,002 at year end, and on a last-twelve-months basis total debt over derived EBITDA was 2.57x in May 2026. The funded debt is long-dated private placement notes and a term loan with no single fiscal year through 2031 above 450,000, while the short-term funding includes securitization and repurchase facilities that now run only to 2027-08-25. Covenants are described only as minimum consolidated net worth and other financial ratios with compliance reported, so headroom is not measurable from these sources. The base supports statement-based credit work; it does not support covenant, ranking or recovery work.

facts.label: Business and transaction view
facts.text: CHS is a member-owned cooperative with no sponsor, no common stock and no pending acquisition, sponsor transaction or new debt issue, so the creditor questions are operating durability and distribution discipline rather than transaction risk. Its three reportable segments are Energy, Grains and Agronomy, with a financing and hedging arm and two minority joint ventures in Corporate and Services; the realignment to a product-line model took effect on 2025-09-01 and recast prior periods. Fiscal 2026 earnings leaned on three things the sources identify: strong refining spreads in Energy, partly cancelled by record renewable fuel compliance costs and helped by a small refinery exemption; oilseed crush and ethanol margins in Grains; and CF Nitrogen in Agronomy, a 7.86% interest that is the largest single source of equity income and sits in a venture CHS does not control. Against that, owner distributions are discretionary, the board cut cash patronage sharply in fiscal 2026 and has authorized an increase for fiscal 2027, and the preferred stock carries no vote. The company announced two large projects, a phosphate joint venture and a soybean plant, both pending approvals and not expected to operate before late 2028; their funding is not described. What the sources do not give is the legal layer: restricted payment capacity, covenant levels, guarantors and ranking. The annual report also contains a seasonality table whose fiscal 2026 fourth quarter share of pretax income (36%) and second quarter share (positive 15%) cannot be reconciled to the filed quarterly statements, which weakens any quarterly trend reading until resolved.

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: No acquisition, sponsor transaction, merger or change of control is described in the sources, and the context lists no deal terms, so there is no transaction to summarize beyond the financing and project events below, each dated and classed by status. In fiscal 2026 the company issued no new notes: the debt table shows only the scheduled repayment of an 80,000 note and the sources state that "We repaid approximately $80.6 million and $331.6 million, respectively, of long-term debt consisting of scheduled debt maturities" for fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2025 (10-K page:164). The one new long-term borrowing was the drawing of the revolving term loan: in the third quarter report the company states "we drew $300.0 million on our revolving term loan facility (the "Facility") for long-term capital planning purposes and utilized the proceeds to reduce short-term amounts outstanding" (10-Q Q3 page:13). That facility is fully drawn, its revolving period ends 2026-10-29 and it then becomes a nonrevolving term loan payable 2029-10-29 (10-K page:165); the scheduled reversion is a subsequent event after the fiscal year end that no later document confirms. On 2026-08-26 the securitization and repurchase facilities were extended to 2027-08-25 (10-K page:164). These are completed events, not proposals. Two announced projects are proposed and conditional: a phosphate production facility of nearly 450 million in Louisiana in a joint venture with OCP North America, and a soybean processing facility of approximately 700 million in Evansville, Wisconsin, with the release stating "Pending project-related approvals, both facilities are expected to be operational in late 2028 or 2029." (Release FY page:2). The 10-K expects fiscal 2027 capital expenditures of approximately 850.8 million including the Evansville plant, and development costs for the phosphate venture, with no financing plan stated (10-K page:76). The company also exited the Producer Ag joint venture on 2025-12-31 for working capital and cash, with no effect on the statement of operations (10-K page:159). The amount of the Producer Ag consideration is not supplied. Use of proceeds, sources and uses, and any new debt issue beyond the term loan are Not supplied because none is described.

facts.label: Capital allocation and disclosure
facts.text: Management states its capital allocation priorities as "paying interest on debt and preferred stock dividends, returning cash to our member-owners in the form of cash patronage and equity redemptions" alongside safety, compliance and strategic opportunities (10-K page:74). Mechanically, the listed order places interest and preferred dividends first and owner returns after, but the order is a management statement and no contractual priority is supplied. The fiscal 2027 plan raises owner cash returns while capital expenditures are expected to rise to approximately 850.8 million from 463.3 million (10-K page:76), so fiscal 2027 cash demands combine growth capital, 168.7 million of preferred dividends, the owner distributions and 58,562 of scheduled debt maturities (CP-1), against a fiscal 2026 operating cash flow of 1,584,009 that CP-1 shows was swollen by working capital timing. No acquisition appetite is inferred from the single phosphate and soybean announcements. What the source set lacks for monitoring is logged in the gaps with severity.

facts.label: Credit view
facts.text: CHS Inc. has a solid fundamental credit profile at the 2026-08-31 balance sheet date, but one that rests on volatile, commodity- and policy-driven earnings rather than steady cash flow. The strongest support is leverage of 1.27x total debt to derived EBITDA, cash interest cover of 11.79x, long-dated unsecured private placement debt with no fiscal year above USD 450.0 million through fiscal 2031, and USD 2,800.0 million of undrawn committed revolver. The weakest point is earnings quality: Energy supplied the whole improvement, about USD 205.0 million came from a refinery exemption, and half of pretax income is equity income from ventures CHS does not control. What decides the outcome is whether refining spreads and nitrogen prices hold while about USD 1,536.1 million of identified fiscal 2027 cash demands are met, and whether covenants not yet seen leave room.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: CHS Inc. entered fiscal 2027 with year-end total debt of USD 2,501.7 million against derived EBITDA of USD 1,969.5 million, a ratio of 1.27x, compared with 2.12x a year earlier (CP-1 C5). The improvement is real but partly seasonal, which the annual figure hides: the fall in total debt of USD 486.6 million, from USD 2,988.3 million, came entirely from notes payable, which fell by USD 703.5 million while long-term debt rose by USD 216.9 million (CP-1A D6), and on a last-twelve-months basis total debt over derived EBITDA was 2.53x, 2.92x and 2.57x at the three interim quarter ends (CP-1 C14). Leverage at the working capital peak is therefore 2.92x, not the 1.27x of the year-end balance sheet.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Earnings improved sharply and narrowly. Pretax income rose to USD 1,128.7 million from USD 614.8 million, and Energy alone moved from a loss of USD 19.0 million to earnings of USD 554.6 million, more than the group improvement of USD 513.9 million (CP-1 C16). Within Energy, the sources identify wider crack spreads and crude discounts, higher throughput, and a small refinery exemption benefit of approximately USD 205.0 million that management says only partially offsets total renewable fuel compliance costs and may not recur (CP-1A, 10-K page:64). Equity income was USD 569.2 million, 50.4% of pretax income (CP-2 E7), of which CF Nitrogen provided USD 406.3 million and USD 447.3 million of cash distributions. The fourth quarter derived from audited year less nine months carried USD 739.3 million of pretax income, and the annual report's own quarterly table disagrees with that split (CP-1A conflicts), so the phasing of the recovery is unverified while the annual totals stand.

facts.text: Cash generation is strong in fiscal 2026 and not flattered by working capital. Operating cash flow was USD 1,584.0 million after a USD 184.0 million net working capital outflow (CP-2 E6), free cash flow after major maintenance was USD 1,052.5 million, and after preferred dividends and owner distributions it was USD 753.4 million (CP-1 C3, C4). facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The forward funding position is adequate but not abundant. Identified fiscal 2027 demands of USD 1,536.1 million comprise capital expenditures of USD 850.8 million, major maintenance of USD 41.8 million, preferred dividends of USD 168.7 million, owner cash returns of USD 315.0 million on the filing figures, scheduled long-term debt maturities of USD 58.6 million and interest on long-term debt of USD 101.3 million (CP-2 E5). That is close to fiscal 2026 operating cash flow of USD 1,584.0 million, so a repeat of fiscal 2026 funds the plan almost exactly, and any shortfall would fall on the USD 2,800.0 million revolver, which is USD 1.40 of capacity for every USD 1.00 of the largest quarter-end notes payable balance of USD 1,995.1 million (CP-2 E8), or on the board's discretion over owner payments. Two announced projects of USD 450 million and USD 700 million are additional and unfunded in the sources.

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Strengths. First, balance sheet and liquidity: year-end leverage of 1.27x, USD 263.6 million of unrestricted cash and USD 2,800.0 million of undrawn committed revolver to 2028-04-21 give CHS Inc. a liquidity base of about USD 3,063.6 million gross of letters of credit that are not supplied (CP-1, CP-2 E9). Second, debt profile: the long-term debt is unsecured private placement notes and a USD 300.0 million term loan, with USD 899.3 million, 44.9% of the total, maturing in the five fiscal years to 2031 and the largest single year at USD 450.0 million (CP-2 E10). Third, a discretionary distribution lever: the board decides the cash portion of patronage and the level of equity redemptions, and cash patronage paid fell from USD 300.4 million to USD 30.0 million between fiscal 2025 and fiscal 2026, so a stress case can release cash without a default event (CP-1A). Fourth, diversification across Energy, Grains and Agronomy, a financing arm and two minority joint ventures. Fifth, demonstrated cash support from CF Nitrogen of USD 447.3 million of distributions in fiscal 2026.

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Weaknesses. First, thin and volatile operating earnings: operating earnings were USD 591.9 million on revenues of USD 39,231.2 million, a margin of 1.5%, and USD 90.8 million in fiscal 2025, so pretax income relies on equity income and other income (CP-1). Second, policy and spread dependence in Energy, where the largest blending obligation ever issued, open-market RIN purchases and a refinery exemption that may not recur all decide margin. Third, concentration: CF Nitrogen provides 71% of equity income (CP-1A D3), a non-controlled venture whose distributions follow nitrogen prices. Fourth, a working capital model that takes quarter-end leverage to 2.92x and ties up large inventory and receivables, with derivative liabilities of USD 546.6 million at year end against USD 178.0 million a year earlier, a mechanic for margin and liquidity calls if commodity prices spike, which the sources do not quantify (CP-1). Fifth, unverifiable structure and covenants: no agreement is supplied. Sixth, growth capital: expected capital expenditure of USD 850.8 million in fiscal 2027 against USD 463.3 million in fiscal 2026 plus two projects with no stated funding. Seventh, a small related-party exposure of USD 10.3 million past due from a director's farm, under Audit Committee-approved terms (CP-1A).

facts.text: CP-1A stated that fiscal 2026 operating cash flow of 1,584,009 was swollen by working capital timing. The CP-1A conflict on the quarterly share table and the CP-0 and CP-1 point on fiscal 2027 redemptions (USD 165.0 million on the filing, against up to USD 150 million in the release) are carried; this module uses the filing.

### Financial base view

CHS Inc. entered fiscal 2026 with modest year-end leverage and finished with a very strong second half, when pretax income was 1,021,508 against 107,211 in the first half (C9). Derived EBITDA of 1,969,497 against total debt of 2,501,725 gives 1.27x at the 2026-08-31 balance sheet date, down from 2.12x a year earlier, and cash paid for interest of 167,057 is covered 11.79x. That picture is flattering in four ways that the base keeps in view. First, the EBITDA is our derivation (pretax income plus interest expense plus depreciation and amortization, including amortization of deferred major maintenance) because the company reports no EBITDA, and it includes 569,231 of equity income from joint ventures and affiliates. Second, nine-month operating earnings were a loss of 12,222 and the fourth quarter derived alone supplied most of the year, so the annual figure is dominated by one quarter. Third, the improvement is concentrated in one segment: Energy improved by 573,605, which exceeds the group improvement of 513,947 because Corporate and Services and Agronomy declined (C16). Fourth, working capital debt is seasonal: notes payable fell from 1,995,108 in February to 449,002 at year end, and on a last-twelve-months basis total debt over derived EBITDA was 2.57x in May 2026. The funded debt is long-dated private placement notes and a term loan with no single fiscal year through 2031 above 450,000, while the short-term funding includes securitization and repurchase facilities that now run only to 2027-08-25. Covenants are described only as minimum consolidated net worth and other financial ratios with compliance reported, so headroom is not measurable from these sources. The base supports statement-based credit work; it does not support covenant, ranking or recovery work.

## Request

This module builds the fact pack a credit committee reads first: the company and its operating model, ownership and governance behaviour, the transactions and financing events of the period, and the points where the sources disagree. Currency is USD; the period is fiscal 2026 (year ended 2026-08-31) with fiscal 2025 comparatives. Figures come from the pinned sources or, where marked, from the CP-1 handoff. No sponsor, acquirer or financing transaction is on the table: the context lists no deal terms, and the sources describe none.

## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| CHS is a farmer-owned cooperative with no sponsor and no pending debt transaction. Its earnings are exposed to refining spreads, fuel-credit costs and one nitrogen venture, and owner distributions are board-discretionary. | Medium | Legal documents, restricted payment capacity and guarantor structure are not supplied, and two sections of the annual report disagree on fourth-quarter earnings. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Energy earnings depend on crack spreads, crude discounts and Renewable Fuel Standard costs, with a small refinery exemption benefit of approximately 205.0 million in fiscal 2026. | Earnings quality in the best year includes a regulatory benefit that is not assured to recur. | High |

| The CF Nitrogen venture produced 406,334 of equity income and 447.3 million of cash distributions in fiscal 2026. | Cash support is concentrated in one non-controlled venture whose results follow nitrogen prices. | High |

| Cash patronage and equity redemptions are decided by the board; cash patronage paid fell from 300,358 in fiscal 2025 to 30,000 in fiscal 2026 (USD thousands). | Owner distributions can be reduced in stress, which supports debt service, but the board decides. | High |

| A director's farm owed 10,260,441 past due at year end, under terms the Audit Committee approved. | Related-party credit exposure is small and disclosed, but shows member-patron overlap in governance. | Medium |

| The annual report's quarterly earnings table shows fourth-quarter pretax income at 36% of the year, while the audited year and the nine-month report imply a much larger share. | Quarterly seasonality cannot be relied on from that table; annual figures stand. | High |
### Business and transaction view

CHS is a member-owned cooperative with no sponsor, no common stock and no pending acquisition, sponsor transaction or new debt issue, so the creditor questions are operating durability and distribution discipline rather than transaction risk. Its three reportable segments are Energy, Grains and Agronomy, with a financing and hedging arm and two minority joint ventures in Corporate and Services; the realignment to a product-line model took effect on 2025-09-01 and recast prior periods. Fiscal 2026 earnings leaned on three things the sources identify: strong refining spreads in Energy, partly cancelled by record renewable fuel compliance costs and helped by a small refinery exemption; oilseed crush and ethanol margins in Grains; and CF Nitrogen in Agronomy, a 7.86% interest that is the largest single source of equity income and sits in a venture CHS does not control. Against that, owner distributions are discretionary, the board cut cash patronage sharply in fiscal 2026 and has authorized an increase for fiscal 2027, and the preferred stock carries no vote. The company announced two large projects, a phosphate joint venture and a soybean plant, both pending approvals and not expected to operate before late 2028; their funding is not described. What the sources do not give is the legal layer: restricted payment capacity, covenant levels, guarantors and ranking. The annual report also contains a seasonality table whose fiscal 2026 fourth quarter share of pretax income (36%) and second quarter share (positive 15%) cannot be reconciled to the filed quarterly statements, which weakens any quarterly trend reading until resolved.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

No acquisition, sponsor transaction, merger or change of control is described in the sources, and the context lists no deal terms, so there is no transaction to summarize beyond the financing and project events below, each dated and classed by status. In fiscal 2026 the company issued no new notes: the debt table shows only the scheduled repayment of an 80,000 note and the sources state that "We repaid approximately $80.6 million and $331.6 million, respectively, of long-term debt consisting of scheduled debt maturities" for fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2025 (10-K page:164). The one new long-term borrowing was the drawing of the revolving term loan: in the third quarter report the company states "we drew $300.0 million on our revolving term loan facility (the "Facility") for long-term capital planning purposes and utilized the proceeds to reduce short-term amounts outstanding" (10-Q Q3 page:13). That facility is fully drawn, its revolving period ends 2026-10-29 and it then becomes a nonrevolving term loan payable 2029-10-29 (10-K page:165); the scheduled reversion is a subsequent event after the fiscal year end that no later document confirms. On 2026-08-26 the securitization and repurchase facilities were extended to 2027-08-25 (10-K page:164). These are completed events, not proposals. Two announced projects are proposed and conditional: a phosphate production facility of nearly 450 million in Louisiana in a joint venture with OCP North America, and a soybean processing facility of approximately 700 million in Evansville, Wisconsin, with the release stating "Pending project-related approvals, both facilities are expected to be operational in late 2028 or 2029." (Release FY page:2). The 10-K expects fiscal 2027 capital expenditures of approximately 850.8 million including the Evansville plant, and development costs for the phosphate venture, with no financing plan stated (10-K page:76). The company also exited the Producer Ag joint venture on 2025-12-31 for working capital and cash, with no effect on the statement of operations (10-K page:159). The amount of the Producer Ag consideration is not supplied. Use of proceeds, sources and uses, and any new debt issue beyond the term loan are Not supplied because none is described.

### Capital allocation and disclosure

Management states its capital allocation priorities as "paying interest on debt and preferred stock dividends, returning cash to our member-owners in the form of cash patronage and equity redemptions" alongside safety, compliance and strategic opportunities (10-K page:74). Mechanically, the listed order places interest and preferred dividends first and owner returns after, but the order is a management statement and no contractual priority is supplied. The fiscal 2027 plan raises owner cash returns while capital expenditures are expected to rise to approximately 850.8 million from 463.3 million (10-K page:76), so fiscal 2027 cash demands combine growth capital, 168.7 million of preferred dividends, the owner distributions and 58,562 of scheduled debt maturities (CP-1), against a fiscal 2026 operating cash flow of 1,584,009 that CP-1 shows was swollen by working capital timing. No acquisition appetite is inferred from the single phosphate and soybean announcements. What the source set lacks for monitoring is logged in the gaps with severity.

| Item | Statement A | Statement B | Downstream effect |

| Quarterly share of fiscal 2026 pretax income | 10-K MD&A seasonality table: "Q4 36 % 30 % 8 % 24 %" and "Q2 15 % (14) % 17 % 6 %" for fiscal 2026, 2025, 2024 and the three-year average (10-K page:60) | 10-Q Q2 reports a second quarter pretax loss of 164,977 (10-Q Q2 page:5) and the 10-Q Q3 reports nine-month pretax income of 389,424 (10-Q Q3 page:5) against the audited year of 1,128,719 (10-K page:144), implying a fourth quarter of 739,295 (CP-1 C9). The filed statements and audited year control. Any reading of quarterly seasonality or of Q4 strength must state the conflict |

| Fiscal 2027 equity redemptions | Release FY: "Company Intends to Return $300 Million Cash to Owners in 2027" (Release FY page:1), described as 150 million cash patronage and up to 150 million redemptions | 10-K Note 12 authorizes 150.0 million of fiscal 2026 redemptions plus an additional 15.0 million for fiscal 2025, both distributed in fiscal 2027 (10-K page:170) | Carried from CP-0 and CP-1: the filing controls; the release headline understates by the additional 15.0 million |
### Credit translations
| Theme | Evidence | Risk mechanic | Credit implication | Conflict that counters it |

| Margin and cash-flow risk in Energy | Crack spreads of $35.15 against $19.91 per barrel and wider crude discounts; refinery throughput of 195,415 against 174,837 barrels per day; exemption benefits of approximately 205.0 million; renewable fuel costs described as record-high | Refining earnings move with crack spreads and crude differentials, and the fuel credit bill (RINs bought on the open market, a rising blending obligation) takes a large share of the margin; a one-off exemption inflates the best year and may not recur or may be clawed back through reallocation | Energy delivered the whole of the fiscal 2026 earnings improvement (CP-1 C16), so debt service capacity and leverage tolerance depend on spreads and regulatory outcomes that management does not control; monitoring posture should track crack spreads, RIN prices and exemption decisions | The seasonality table conflict limits any quarterly read of how the Energy recovery phased |

| Concentration in one non-controlled venture | CF Nitrogen equity income of 406,334 within total equity income of 569,231 (CP-1) and cash distributions of 447.3 million; three customers, one of them CHS | Upstream cash depends on distributions set under the venture's LLC agreement and on urea and UAN prices; CHS does not control the venture and its debt service is not a claim on the venture's assets | Equity income and distributions support coverage, but they are not controlled cash flows; a nitrogen price fall would reduce earnings and the distribution that supports the owners' and preferred payments | None logged |

| Distribution flexibility | Board discretion over cash patronage and redemptions; cash patronage cut from 300,358 to 30,000; retention of 35% of patronage earnings | The largest discretionary outflow can be cut without a default event, and equity certificates are redeemed only at board discretion | Distribution flexibility is a liquidity buffer for debt service in a downturn, subject to member relations and the board's choices | The fiscal 2027 plan raises distributions while capital expenditures rise |

| Sponsor and control alignment | No sponsor; member-elected board; preferred holders have no vote; related-party dealings customary and disclosed | Control sits with patron-members whose interests as suppliers and customers of CHS are not those of creditors; no leveraged-buyout style extraction is documented | Alignment with creditors is neutral; absence of a sponsor removes recapitalisation risk but also any sponsor support | None logged |

CP-1 stated that the sources give no discrete fourth-quarter commentary and presented the derived fourth quarter of 739,295 without noting that the 10-K contains a quarterly pretax earnings table (10-K page:60) whose fiscal 2026 second and fourth quarter shares disagree with it. The percentages in D2 to D4 are rounded to whole numbers; D4 uses an approximate benefit and is indicative only.

Proceed to CP-2 with these carried items: Energy margin and fuel-credit exposure including the approximately 205.0 million exemption benefit; CF Nitrogen concentration and distributions; the discretionary distribution lever and the fiscal 2027 plan, with the filing figure for redemptions; the pending, unfunded projects; the unresolved seasonality table conflict; and the absence of the legal layer. ## Findings
### Reader summary

| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Total debt was USD 2,501.7 million at 2026-08-31, 1.27x derived EBITDA, and fell from USD 2,988.3 million, all through lower short-term borrowing. | Year-end leverage is at a seasonal low; quarter-end leverage reached 2.92x in February 2026. | High |

| Identified fiscal 2027 cash demands are about USD 1,536.1 million, close to fiscal 2026 operating cash flow of USD 1,584.0 million. | The plan relies on earnings repeating; the shortfall would fall on the revolver or on discretionary owner payments. | Medium |

| Energy supplied the whole earnings improvement, including about USD 205.0 million from a refinery exemption, and equity income is 50.4% of pretax income. | Earnings quality is exposed to refining spreads, fuel credit costs, regulation and one nitrogen venture. | High |

| Committed revolver capacity is USD 2,800.0 million, undrawn at year end, and no long-term maturity exceeds USD 450.0 million in any year through fiscal 2031. | Refinancing pressure is modest for term debt; the short-term facilities expire by 2027-08-25. | Medium |
### Credit view

CHS Inc. has a solid fundamental credit profile at the 2026-08-31 balance sheet date, but one that rests on volatile, commodity- and policy-driven earnings rather than steady cash flow. The strongest support is leverage of 1.27x total debt to derived EBITDA, cash interest cover of 11.79x, long-dated unsecured private placement debt with no fiscal year above USD 450.0 million through fiscal 2031, and USD 2,800.0 million of undrawn committed revolver. The weakest point is earnings quality: Energy supplied the whole improvement, about USD 205.0 million came from a refinery exemption, and half of pretax income is equity income from ventures CHS does not control. What decides the outcome is whether refining spreads and nitrogen prices hold while about USD 1,536.1 million of identified fiscal 2027 cash demands are met, and whether covenants not yet seen leave room.
### Key findings

CHS Inc. entered fiscal 2027 with year-end total debt of USD 2,501.7 million against derived EBITDA of USD 1,969.5 million, a ratio of 1.27x, compared with 2.12x a year earlier (CP-1 C5). The improvement is real but partly seasonal, which the annual figure hides: the fall in total debt of USD 486.6 million, from USD 2,988.3 million, came entirely from notes payable, which fell by USD 703.5 million while long-term debt rose by USD 216.9 million (CP-1A D6), and on a last-twelve-months basis total debt over derived EBITDA was 2.53x, 2.92x and 2.57x at the three interim quarter ends (CP-1 C14). Leverage at the working capital peak is therefore 2.92x, not the 1.27x of the year-end balance sheet.

Earnings improved sharply and narrowly. Pretax income rose to USD 1,128.7 million from USD 614.8 million, and Energy alone moved from a loss of USD 19.0 million to earnings of USD 554.6 million, more than the group improvement of USD 513.9 million (CP-1 C16). Within Energy, the sources identify wider crack spreads and crude discounts, higher throughput, and a small refinery exemption benefit of approximately USD 205.0 million that management says only partially offsets total renewable fuel compliance costs and may not recur (CP-1A, 10-K page:64). Equity income was USD 569.2 million, 50.4% of pretax income (CP-2 E7), of which CF Nitrogen provided USD 406.3 million and USD 447.3 million of cash distributions. The fourth quarter derived from audited year less nine months carried USD 739.3 million of pretax income, and the annual report's own quarterly table disagrees with that split (CP-1A conflicts), so the phasing of the recovery is unverified while the annual totals stand.

Cash generation is strong in fiscal 2026 and not flattered by working capital. Operating cash flow was USD 1,584.0 million after a USD 184.0 million net working capital outflow (CP-2 E6), free cash flow after major maintenance was USD 1,052.5 million, and after preferred dividends and owner distributions it was USD 753.4 million (CP-1 C3, C4). This corrects CP-1A, which described operating cash flow as helped by working capital timing. In fiscal 2025 free cash flow after distributions was negative USD 1,120.9 million, so cash generation moved by USD 1,874.3 million between adjacent years (CP-2 E11).

Fixed charges are covered but the margin depends on the earnings base. EBITDA covers cash interest plus preferred dividends 5.87x in fiscal 2026 against 4.47x in fiscal 2025, and on the narrower operating EBITDA measure the cover is 3.78x against 2.35x (CP-2 E1, E2). Adding operating lease liabilities of USD 237.5 million gives 1.39x leverage, and treating the preferred stock at its redemption value of USD 2,273.3 million as a debt-like fixed claim gives 2.42x (CP-2 E3, E4), an analytical adjustment and not a statement of legal ranking.

The forward funding position is adequate but not abundant. Identified fiscal 2027 demands of USD 1,536.1 million comprise capital expenditures of USD 850.8 million, major maintenance of USD 41.8 million, preferred dividends of USD 168.7 million, owner cash returns of USD 315.0 million on the filing figures, scheduled long-term debt maturities of USD 58.6 million and interest on long-term debt of USD 101.3 million (CP-2 E5). That is close to fiscal 2026 operating cash flow of USD 1,584.0 million, so a repeat of fiscal 2026 funds the plan almost exactly, and any shortfall would fall on the USD 2,800.0 million revolver, which is USD 1.40 of capacity for every USD 1.00 of the largest quarter-end notes payable balance of USD 1,995.1 million (CP-2 E8), or on the board's discretion over owner payments. Two announced projects of USD 450 million and USD 700 million are additional and unfunded in the sources.

What cannot be concluded: covenant headroom, because the net worth and ratio tests are described but no level is printed; the effect of letters of credit on revolver availability; structural position of creditors, because guarantors and security are not stated; and ratings and market pricing, which are out of scope.
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strengths. First, balance sheet and liquidity: year-end leverage of 1.27x, USD 263.6 million of unrestricted cash and USD 2,800.0 million of undrawn committed revolver to 2028-04-21 give CHS Inc. a liquidity base of about USD 3,063.6 million gross of letters of credit that are not supplied (CP-1, CP-2 E9). Second, debt profile: the long-term debt is unsecured private placement notes and a USD 300.0 million term loan, with USD 899.3 million, 44.9% of the total, maturing in the five fiscal years to 2031 and the largest single year at USD 450.0 million (CP-2 E10). Third, a discretionary distribution lever: the board decides the cash portion of patronage and the level of equity redemptions, and cash patronage paid fell from USD 300.4 million to USD 30.0 million between fiscal 2025 and fiscal 2026, so a stress case can release cash without a default event (CP-1A). Fourth, diversification across Energy, Grains and Agronomy, a financing arm and two minority joint ventures. Fifth, demonstrated cash support from CF Nitrogen of USD 447.3 million of distributions in fiscal 2026.

Weaknesses. First, thin and volatile operating earnings: operating earnings were USD 591.9 million on revenues of USD 39,231.2 million, a margin of 1.5%, and USD 90.8 million in fiscal 2025, so pretax income relies on equity income and other income (CP-1). Second, policy and spread dependence in Energy, where the largest blending obligation ever issued, open-market RIN purchases and a refinery exemption that may not recur all decide margin. Third, concentration: CF Nitrogen provides 71% of equity income (CP-1A D3), a non-controlled venture whose distributions follow nitrogen prices. Fourth, a working capital model that takes quarter-end leverage to 2.92x and ties up large inventory and receivables, with derivative liabilities of USD 546.6 million at year end against USD 178.0 million a year earlier, a mechanic for margin and liquidity calls if commodity prices spike, which the sources do not quantify (CP-1). Fifth, unverifiable structure and covenants: no agreement is supplied. Sixth, growth capital: expected capital expenditure of USD 850.8 million in fiscal 2027 against USD 463.3 million in fiscal 2026 plus two projects with no stated funding. Seventh, a small related-party exposure of USD 10.3 million past due from a director's farm, under Audit Committee-approved terms (CP-1A).
### Credit assessment
| Dimension | View | Category | Basis |

| Business risk | Moderate: diversified cooperative with scale and member channels, but low operating margin and heavy exposure to commodity spreads and policy | Analyst Interpretation | CP-1A operating model and credit translations; CP-1 C16 |
| Financial risk | Low to moderate on year-end leverage, moderate at the seasonal peak | Analyst Interpretation | CP-1 C5, C14; CP-2 E3, E4 |

| Liquidity | Adequate: cash plus undrawn revolver exceed the largest quarter-end short-term borrowing, near-term maturities are small, short-term facilities expire by 2027-08-25 | Analyst Interpretation | CP-1 liquidity register; CP-2 E8, E9 |
| Structure and covenants | Not assessable: agreements, covenant levels, guarantors and security not supplied | Insufficient Information | CP-0 and CP-1 gaps |
| Governance and ownership | Neutral: member-elected board, no sponsor, discretionary distributions, disclosed related-party dealings | Analyst Interpretation | CP-1A governance table |
| Overall fundamental view | Solid but cyclical; strength rests on Energy spreads, a regulatory benefit and one nitrogen venture; confidence Medium | Analyst Interpretation | All of the above |
### Key credit risks
| Risk | Mechanic | Credit implication | Severity |

| Energy margin reversal | Crack spreads, crude discounts or the exemption benefit fall while renewable fuel credit costs stay high | Pretax income could revert toward fiscal 2025 levels (USD 614.8 million) and fixed charge cover toward 4.47x | Material |

| Nitrogen price and distribution risk | CF Nitrogen distributions follow urea and UAN prices and the LLC agreement; CHS does not control the venture | Loss of equity income and cash support reduces coverage; the cash is not controlled by creditors | Material |

| Seasonal and commodity-driven borrowing peaks | Inventory, receivables and margin calls lift short-term debt to USD 1,995.1 million and derivative liabilities rose | Quarter-end leverage 2.92x; a price spike combined with weak earnings could press the revolver | Material |

| Fiscal 2027 cash demand | Capital expenditure, preferred dividends and owner returns absorb about the whole of fiscal 2026 operating cash flow | Little room for earnings shortfall without drawing on the revolver or cutting owner payments | Material |
| Unseen covenants and structure | Net worth and ratio tests, guarantee limits and restricted payments are not supplied | Headroom and creditor ranking cannot be verified | Material |
| Data conflict in annual report | Quarterly share table disagrees with filed statements | Quarterly phasing of the recovery is unverified | Minor |

| Related-party and governance | Member-directors are customers and suppliers; USD 10.3 million past due from a director's farm | Small, disclosed and approved; shows overlap rather than leakage | Minor |
### Corrections to upstream handoffs

CP-1A stated that fiscal 2026 operating cash flow of 1,584,009 was swollen by working capital timing. The cash flow statement shows the opposite: receivables, inventories, payables and other lines together used USD 184.0 million in fiscal 2026 and USD 464.4 million in fiscal 2025 (CP-2 E6; 10-K page:146), so fiscal 2026 operating cash flow was not flattered by a working capital release. CP-1A's related remark that free cash flow swings with working capital is true of the year-on-year change only in part: the swing between fiscal 2025 and fiscal 2026 also reflects higher earnings and lower capital spending. No other statement in CP-0, CP-1 or CP-1A is changed. The CP-1A conflict on the quarterly share table and the CP-0 and CP-1 point on fiscal 2027 redemptions (USD 165.0 million on the filing, against up to USD 150 million in the release) are carried; this module uses the filing.
## Calculations
USD thousands unless stated; ratios are rounded to two decimals. Inputs marked CP-1 are as printed in that handoff.
| Id | Calculation | Inputs | Result |

| E4 | (Total debt + preferred redemption values) / EBITDA, FY2026 only | (2,501,725 + 2,273,300) / 1,969,497 = 4,775,025 / 1,969,497; redemption values total USD 2,273.3 million (CP-1 C11); FY2025 redemption values not stated | 2.42 |

| E5 | Identified fiscal 2027 cash demands (USD millions) | Capital expenditures 850.8 + major maintenance 41.8 (10-K page:76) + preferred dividends 168.7 (10-K page:76) + cash patronage 150.0 + equity redemptions 165.0 (10-K page:170) + long-term debt maturities 58.562 + interest on long-term debt 101.271 (10-K page:77); against fiscal 2026 operating cash flow 1,584.009 | 1,536.133; ratio to fiscal 2026 operating cash flow 0.97. On the release basis (redemptions 150.0): 1,521.133 |

| E6 | Working capital change in operating cash flow, sum of receivables, inventories, accounts payable and accrued expenses, and other, net (10-K page:146) | FY2026: (150,562) + (455,758) + 359,133 + 63,180; FY2025: 6,999 + (53,184) + (276,114) + (142,098); FY2024: (335,974) + 147,764 + (213,788) + 77,638 | (184,007); (464,397); (324,360) |
| E7 | Equity income share of pretax income = 569,231 / 1,128,719; Energy share = 554,590 / 1,128,719 | 10-K page:144, page:181 | 50.4%; 49.1% |

| E8 | Revolver commitment over the largest quarter-end notes payable | 2,800.0 / 1,995.108 (USD millions; February 2026 notes payable CP-1 C14); some of that borrowing may sit outside the revolver | 1.40 |
| E9 | Gross liquidity at 2026-08-31 = cash + undrawn committed revolver | 263.603 + 2,800.0 (USD millions); letters of credit not supplied | 3,063.603 |
| E11 | Change in free cash flow after owner and preferred distributions, fiscal 2026 against fiscal 2025 | 753,391 - (1,120,877) (CP-1 C4) | 1,874,268 (USD 1,874.3 million) |

Recomputation notes: E5 treats owner cash returns on the filing figures and excludes operating lease payments and tax, which sit within operating cash flow; the demands exclude the two announced projects and any change in working capital.
